[Cough | Overview]
A cough is your body's way of clearing foreign substances and mucus from your lungs and upper airway passages. Coughs can either be productive, meaning they bring up phlegm or mucus, or non-productive (dry), producing no secretions. Most acute coughs are caused by viral respiratory infections such as the common cold, acute bronchitis, or influenza. Chronic coughs, defined as coughs that last longer than eight weeks in adults or four weeks in children, are frequently caused by asthma, postnasal drip from allergic rhinitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), or environmental irritants such as tobacco smoke.

[Cough | Home Management And Relief]
Staying well-hydrated helps thin secretions in your throat and airways, making it easier to cough up phlegm. Drinking warm fluids such as herbal teas, warm lemon water with honey, or clear broths can soothe irritation in the throat. (Note: honey should never be given to infants under one year of age due to the risk of infant botulism). Using a cool-mist humidifier or inhaling steam from a warm shower can moisten dry airways and relieve nighttime coughing fits. Elevating your head with extra pillows while sleeping can prevent postnasal drip from triggering throat spasms.

[Cough | When To See A Doctor]
You should seek emergency medical care immediately if you experience shortness of breath, wheezing, coughing up pink frothy phlegm or bright red blood, severe chest tightness, or a bluish discoloration of the lips or face. Consult a doctor if an unexplained cough persists for more than three weeks, is accompanied by unexplained weight loss or night sweats, or makes speaking in full sentences difficult.

[Fever | Overview]
A fever is a temporary increase in your body temperature, often due to an illness. Having a fever is a sign that something out of the ordinary is going on in your body. For an adult, a fever may be uncomfortable, but usually it isn't a cause for concern unless it reaches 103 F (39.4 C) or higher. For infants and toddlers, a slightly elevated temperature may indicate a serious infection. Fevers generally go away within a few days. A number of over-the-counter medications lower a fever, but sometimes it is better left untreated because a fever seems to play a key role in helping your body fight off a number of infections.

[Fever | Common Symptoms]
You have a fever when your temperature rises above its normal range. What is normal for you may be a little higher or lower than the average normal temperature of 98.6 F (37 C). Depending on what is causing your fever, additional fever signs and symptoms may include sweating, chills and shivering, headache, muscle aches, loss of appetite, irritability, and general weakness. Dehydration is also common during fevers because the body loses fluids through sweat and increased respiration. Young children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years might experience febrile seizures during sudden high fevers.

[Fever | Home Care And Hydration]
In most cases, drinking plenty of fluids is the most important self-care measure. Water, clear broths, and oral rehydration solutions help prevent dehydration. Resting is vital because physical activity can raise your body temperature. Staying in a comfortable, cool room and wearing lightweight clothing helps your body dissipate heat naturally. Do not bundle up in heavy blankets even if you experience chills, as this can trap body heat and push your internal temperature higher. Tepid sponging with lukewarm water can provide comfort, but cold baths or alcohol rubs should never be used.

[Fever | When To See A Doctor]
Seek immediate medical attention if a fever is accompanied by a severe headache, stiff neck, shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, persistent vomiting, or a sudden unexplained rash. For infants under 3 months old, any rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher requires immediate emergency evaluation by a pediatrician, even if the infant exhibits no other signs of illness. For adults, consult a healthcare provider if a fever lasts longer than three consecutive days or repeatedly spikes above 103 F despite home measures.

[Headache | Overview]
A headache is pain or discomfort in the head, scalp, or neck. Most headaches are primary headaches, meaning they are not a symptom of an underlying disease. The most common primary headaches include tension-type headaches, migraines, and cluster headaches. Tension headaches produce dull, aching head pain often described as a tight band around the forehead. Migraines typically involve pulsing or throbbing pain, usually on one side of the head, and are frequently accompanied by sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, or visual auras.

[Headache | Home Management And Prevention]
Many tension headaches improve with relaxation techniques, stress reduction, adequate sleep, and maintaining regular meal schedules to prevent blood sugar drops. Applying a cold cloth or ice pack wrapped in a towel to the forehead or temples can help numb migraine pain, while gentle heat on the neck can relax tight muscles in tension headaches. Resting quietly in a dark, quiet room during an episode is often beneficial.

[Headache | When To See A Doctor]
Seek urgent emergency care if you experience a sudden, explosive headache (often described as the worst headache of your life, known as a thunderclap headache), a headache accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, seizure, double vision, numbness, or difficulty speaking. You should also seek urgent evaluation if a headache follows a recent head injury, or if a new headache pattern develops in someone over age 50.

[Acidity And Gerd | Overview]
Acidity, clinically known as acid reflux or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), occurs when stomach acid frequently flows back into the tube connecting your mouth and stomach (esophagus). This backwash of acid can irritate the delicate lining of your esophagus. While occasional acid reflux is very common, chronic reflux occurring more than twice a week can lead to complications such as esophageal inflammation or strictures.

[Acidity And Gerd | Common Symptoms]
A burning sensation in your chest (heartburn), usually occurring after eating and potentially worse at night or while lying down, is the hallmark symptom. Other symptoms include regurgitation of sour or bitter-tasting liquid into the throat, upper abdominal discomfort, difficulty swallowing, a sensation of a lump in your throat, and chronic dry cough or hoarseness in the morning.

[Acidity And Gerd | Dietary And Lifestyle Measures]
Lifestyle adjustments are the first line of management for mild acidity. Helpful practices include eating smaller, more frequent meals rather than large heavy dinners; avoiding lying down for at least 2 to 3 hours after eating; elevating the head of your bed by 6 inches; avoiding tight clothing that puts pressure on the abdomen; maintaining a healthy weight; and moderating consumption of known trigger foods such as deeply fried foods, oily gravies, excess caffeine, carbonated drinks, citrus fruits, and spicy dishes.

[Acidity And Gerd | Distinguishing From Cardiac Emergencies]
It is vital to distinguish between harmless heartburn and serious cardiac events. If chest pain radiates to your left arm, shoulder, jaw, neck, or back, or is accompanied by shortness of breath, cold sweat, lightheadedness, or sudden nausea, treat it immediately as a potential heart emergency and call 112 / 108. Never assume chest pain with radiating discomfort is merely acidity.

[Diarrhoea And Dehydration | Overview]
Diarrhoea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or liquid stools per day, or more frequently than is normal for the individual. Frequent passing of formed stools is not diarrhoea. Diarrhoea is typically a symptom of an infection in the intestinal tract, which can be caused by a variety of bacterial, viral, and parasitic organisms. The most critical threat posed by acute diarrhoea is dehydration, which occurs when water and essential electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate) are lost through liquid stools, vomit, sweat, and urine.

[Diarrhoea And Dehydration | Recognizing Dehydration]
Mild to moderate dehydration presents with dry mouth and tongue, sunken eyes, decreased skin elasticity (pinched skin goes back slowly), intense thirst, reduced urine output, and dark-colored urine. In severe dehydration, symptoms progress to extreme lethargy or unconsciousness, very low blood pressure, rapid and weak pulse, cool and moist extremities, and inability to drink fluids. Severe dehydration is life-threatening, especially in infants, young children, and elderly individuals.

[Diarrhoea And Dehydration | Oral Rehydration Therapy]
The cornerstone of diarrhoea management is immediate oral rehydration therapy using standard Oral Rehydration Salt (ORS) solution mixed in safe drinking water. In home settings where commercial ORS packets are temporarily unavailable, homemade sugar-salt solution (6 level teaspoons of sugar and half level teaspoon of salt dissolved in 1 litre of clean boiled water) or clean rice water, coconut water, and diluted buttermilk can be administered continuously after each loose stool. Nutritious, easily digestible foods like khichdi, bananas, and curd should continue to be offered. Do not withhold food during diarrhoeal illness.

[Diarrhoea And Dehydration | When To See A Doctor]
Seek urgent hospital care if loose stools contain visible blood, if vomiting is continuous preventing fluid retention, if high fever develops, if diarrhoea lasts longer than 48 hours without improvement, or if the individual exhibits signs of severe dehydration such as confusion, unresponsiveness, or absence of urination for over 8 hours.

[Dengue Awareness | Overview]
Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti. The virus is widespread throughout the tropics, with local variations in risk influenced by rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, and rapid unplanned urbanization. While most people who get dengue experience mild or no symptoms, in some individuals the virus can cause severe dengue, a potentially lethal complication that requires urgent hospital management.

[Dengue Awareness | Symptoms And Warning Signs]
Mild dengue manifests with a sudden onset of high fever (40 C / 104 F) accompanied by at least two of the following: severe headache, pain behind the eyes (retro-orbital pain), muscle and joint aches (sometimes called breakbone fever), nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, and rash. Symptoms usually appear 4 to 10 days after infection and last for 2 to 7 days. Severe dengue warning signs typically emerge 3 to 7 days after illness onset, often around the time the fever drops below 38 C. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, mucosal bleeding (bleeding gums or nose), fluid accumulation, fatigue, restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool. Severe dengue is a medical emergency due to plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, respiratory distress, and organ impairment.

[Dengue Awareness | Care And Prevention]
There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue fever. Supportive home care focuses on plenty of bed rest and aggressive oral rehydration with clean water, oral rehydration salts (ORS), and fruit juices to replace electrolytes lost to fever and vomiting. Avoiding mosquito bites during illness is crucial to prevent transmitting the virus to household contacts. Use mosquito nets, window screens, and wear clothing that minimizes skin exposure.

[Dengue Awareness | When To Seek Emergency Care]
If you or someone in your care displays any warning signs of severe dengue—such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, difficulty breathing, or severe lethargy—go to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately. Prompt medical assessment and intravenous fluid administration by trained healthcare professionals reduce dengue mortality rates to below 1 percent.

[Hypertension Awareness | Overview]
Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, is a common condition in which the blood vessels have persistently raised pressure. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: systolic (pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (pressure when the heart rests between beats). Hypertension is diagnosed if, when measured on two different days, the systolic blood pressure reading on both days is 140 mmHg or greater and the diastolic reading is 90 mmHg or greater. Hypertension is commonly referred to as a silent killer because most people who have high blood pressure show no warning signs or symptoms until serious organ damage has already occurred.

[Hypertension Awareness | Symptoms And Complications]
Most individuals with high blood pressure do not feel sick. However, very high blood pressure can cause early morning headaches, nosebleeds, irregular heart rhythms, vision changes, and buzzing in the ears (tinnitus). Severe hypertension may cause fatigue, nausea, vomiting, confusion, anxiety, chest pain, and muscle tremors. If left unmanaged, hypertension damages arterial walls and can lead to severe cardiovascular events such as heart attacks, heart failure, strokes, kidney damage, and vascular dementia.

[Hypertension Awareness | Lifestyle Modifications]
Lifestyle changes play a foundational role in preventing and managing high blood pressure. Key evidence-based modifications include reducing dietary sodium intake to less than 2 grams per day (equivalent to under 5 grams of salt), eating more fresh vegetables and fruits, engaging in regular physical activity such as brisk walking for at least 30 minutes five days a week, avoiding tobacco use, moderating alcohol consumption, and effectively managing chronic mental stress.

[Hypertension Awareness | When To Seek Emergency Care]
A hypertensive crisis occurs when blood pressure spikes to 180/120 mmHg or higher. If a high blood pressure reading is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision, or difficulty speaking, emergency medical services (such as 112 or 108) must be contacted immediately. Do not attempt to manage a hypertensive crisis at home.
